Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home

Memory.value: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
issues.explanation: A needles/medical visual trigger is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner unless there is clear trauma-related medical treatment, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere in threat, memory, appraisals, or strategies. The rest of the profile centers on interpersonal danger and intrusion rather than medical trauma cues, so this trigger appears clinically mismatched.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event
issues.explanation: 'Avoid site of the event' is difficult to interpret coherently for ongoing or domestic partner abuse in this profile. If the abuse occurred in shared/home spaces, the profile would usually show corresponding location-specific triggers or avoidance themes; instead the threat items focus on general vigilance and home intrusion, making this item feel insufficiently anchored to the rest of the selected content.

vignette:
Bao, at twenty-four, had come to believe that safety was an illusion, a story people told themselves between disasters. He spends most of his days in his small painting studio, the scent of turpentine a constant, sharp comfort. Six months have passed since he left his ex-partner, but the event that ended their relationship does not feel like it is in the past. It lives in the present, replaying itself in disjointed, searingly bright fragments. He can recall with perfect, photographic detail the way his ex-partner's knuckles whitened as he gripped a heavy glass frame—one of Bao's own pieces—but he cannot remember what they were arguing about. The memory jumps from that image to the sound of shattering glass, and then to the cold shock of the kitchen tile against his cheek. He knows there are missing pieces, entire minutes that are just a void, and the inability to string the moments into a coherent sequence makes him feel like he is losing his mind. When these images surge up, unbidden, it is not like watching a film; he is there again, feeling the floorboards vibrate with heavy footsteps, his body tensing for an impact he can’t place in time.

In the months since, Bao has constructed a life of careful routines designed to keep the world at a manageable distance. He rarely leaves his studio apartment before noon and always ensures he is home before dark. When he does go out for supplies, he feels a prickling sensation on his neck, a certainty that he is being observed, his movements tracked. He finds himself automatically mapping every new space he enters, his eyes immediately flicking to find all possible exits before he can even register what is on the walls or who is in the room. This vigilance extends to his phone; if his current partner, Leo, takes more than a few minutes to reply to a text, a cold dread washes over him. Uncertainty of any kind has become a potent threat, a sign that the fragile order he has built is about to collapse. Back in his apartment, the building’s normal groans and settling sounds become sinister. He listens constantly for the specific scrape of a key in the lock, the soft tread of footsteps in the hall, monitoring for any sign of intrusion.

These behaviours have reshaped his life. He once loved the vibrant, chaotic energy of gallery openings, but now the thought of a crowded room is unbearable. He has come to believe that what happened was a direct result of who he is—that some deep-seated inadequacy or flaw in his character invited the violence. This conviction has hollowed out his sense of self, leaving him feeling like an outsider in his own life, a person who no longer belongs anywhere, not with his old friends, and certainly not in the art world he once cherished. His work, once his greatest source of pride, now feels like a testament to this failure. He paints through the night, not from a place of inspiration, but in a frantic effort to outrun the nightmares that ambush him the moment he drifts off to sleep.

The decision to seek help came after an incident with Leo. His new partner is gentle and patient, but Bao’s world has shrunk to a size that barely includes himself, let alone another person. A few nights ago, Leo came up behind him while he was washing brushes and wrapped his arms around his waist in a quiet hug. Bao did not scream or pull away. He simply froze, his body becoming rigid and unresponsive, his breath caught in his chest. In that moment, he wasn't in his studio with the man he was learning to love; he was back in the old apartment, cornered and silent. The look of confusion and hurt on Leo’s face when he finally turned around was what broke through his paralysis. Bao is terrified of losing this new, tentative peace, but even more terrifying is the thought that he is fundamentally broken, that the person he was before the event is gone for good. He has come to therapy hoping to find a way to exist in the present moment without the past constantly crashing in.
